definition.text: Natural resource management is the managing of land, water, soil, plants and animals with attention to how it affects life for people now and in the future.

facts.text: It deals with how people and natural landscapes interact, recognizing that livelihoods depend on healthy, productive land.
It brings together heritage protection, land-use planning, water management, biodiversity conservation and the future of farming, mining, tourism, fishing and forestry.
In the 20th century people saw that strict preservation had not stopped resources declining, so a more integrated approach took in social, economic and political sides.
Its issues are complex and contested: natural cycles are linked, and a change in one can have long-lasting, even irreversible, effects.
Managers must also weigh many stakeholders, policies, politics, borders and economic effects.
Tools such as GIS help by overlaying data sets, for example rainfall, cleared land and erosion, to plan bush regeneration.

definition.text: Resource management approaches can be grouped by who holds rights over a resource: the state, a private owner, a group, no one, or a mix.

facts.text: Under state property the state owns and controls the resource, and others use it only with permission, as in US national forests and parks.
Under private property a defined person or company owns the resource and bears both its benefits and its duties.
Common property is in effect the private property of a group, such as a community forest.
Open-access resources have no owner, anyone may use them, and they are the most exploited; a lake fishery is an example.
Many real cases are hybrids, such as native vegetation in New South Wales, protected in the public interest but mostly on private land.

definition.text: Stakeholder analysis identifies the different interest groups affected by how natural resources are used and conserved.

facts.text: Borrowed from business management, it is hard to apply because it is difficult to say who has a stake in a resource.
Its stages include identifying decision-makers and stakeholders, investigating their interests, and mapping conflicts, trade-offs and synergies.
A proposal to represent nature itself as a stakeholder has been rejected by many scholars as hard to put into practice.

title: Community-based natural resource management
article: Natural resource management#Community-based natural resource management

definition.text: Community-based natural resource management combines conservation goals with economic benefits for rural communities.

facts.text: It assumes locals are best placed to conserve resources, that people conserve only when benefits exceed costs, and that they protect what is tied to their quality of life.
It rests on subsidiarity, the principle of handling decisions at the most local level that can manage them.
Critics such as Tania Murray found that in upland Southeast Asia it could force communities to meet discriminatory conditions before gaining legal rights to resources.
Social capital and gender shape how it works in practice.

title: Integrated natural resource management
article: Natural resource management#Integrated natural resource management

definition.text: Integrated natural resource management manages resources systematically, balancing biophysical, political and economic aspects to meet both users' production goals and wider community goals.

facts.text: It focuses on sustainability and brings all stakeholders in from the planning stage to reduce later conflict.
It grew out of research on sustainable land use, participatory planning, integrated watershed management and adaptive management.

definition.text: Adaptive management is a step-by-step, repeated way of making decisions under uncertainty that reduces that uncertainty over time by monitoring the system.

facts.text: Each decision both pursues management goals and gathers information to improve future management.
Its challenge is balancing learning for the future against getting the best short-term result with what is known now.
Australian catchment authorities use it as their main method, following a 'plan-do-review-act' cycle.
It is one of the recommended ways to manage biodiversity with precaution, because it tackles the uncertainty of complex systems.

definition.text: The commons are the cultural and natural resources open to all members of a society, such as air, water and a habitable Earth.

facts.text: Commons can also mean resources that a group of users governs for themselves, through rules they create, rather than through the state or the market.
The word comes from the old English legal term for common land, and Garrett Hardin's 1968 article 'The Tragedy of the Commons' made it a general term for shared resources.
Before Hardin's article, academic titles mentioning 'the commons' or 'common property' were very rare.
In Mongolia, where herders moved collectively between pastures, grassland degradation was about 9%, against about 75% in Russia and 33% in China under state or household pastures.
Nepal handed forest control to communities from the late 1980s, giving locals a financial stake that encourages them to prevent overuse.
Globalization brings new pressures: resources like fish and timber are sold on world markets, making impacts harder for local communities to monitor.

definition.text: A set of rules Elinor Ostrom found in commons that are governed successfully, such as clear boundaries, monitoring and graduated sanctions.

facts.text: Early tragedy-of-the-commons work suggested all commons were doomed, but later economists found many successful ones, and Ostrom won the Nobel Prize for analysing them.
Ostrom found that farmers have run grazing commons in the Swiss Alps successfully for hundreds of years.
Her principles are clear boundaries, rules fitted to local conditions, collective choice, monitoring, graduated sanctions, conflict resolution, recognised rights to organize and nested enterprises.
The principles work best when more than nine are used together.
The related 'comedy of the commons', coined by Carol M. Rose in 1986, describes users policing their own use to keep or improve a commons.

definition.text: Commoning treats the commons as an ongoing practice, the process of people coming together to manage shared resources, rather than as a thing.

facts.text: Some authors separate the shared resources, the community that governs them, and commoning, the act of managing them together.
In farming, commoning is the joint stewardship of shared land, and it matters to food systems in many communities worldwide.

definition.text: Urban commons are city resources managed by citizens themselves, valued by their use and upkeep costs rather than their market price.

facts.text: David Harvey argued that public spaces are not automatically commons; they become commons when citizens take political action there.
Urban commons work alongside the state and the market rather than replacing them.
